Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

## Verification of Your Submitted Information

All three items you provided check out:

- **Title:** Correct — "Current Employment Statistics (CES)," also commonly called the *establishment survey* or *payroll survey*.
- **Description:** Correct — it matches BLS's own boilerplate nearly verbatim: "a monthly survey conducted by the Bureau of Labor Statistics [that] provides employment, hours, and earnings estimates based on payroll records of business establishments."
- **URL:** Correct — https://www.bls.gov/ces is the program's official homepage (national estimates). State/metro data live at https://www.bls.gov/sae/.

---

## 1. What the Dataset Is

CES is one of the oldest and most-watched federal statistical programs in the world. Each month it surveys roughly **119,000 businesses and government agencies representing approximately 622,000–629,000 individual worksites** — a sample covering about **one-third of all nonfarm payroll jobs** in the United States. From respondents' payroll records, BLS produces monthly estimates of:

- **Employment** — nonfarm wage-and-salary jobs, for all employees (AE), production and nonsupervisory employees (PE), and women employees (WE)
- **Hours** — average weekly hours (AWH); average weekly overtime hours (AWOH) for manufacturing only; indexes of aggregate hours
- **Earnings** — average hourly earnings (AHE) and average weekly earnings, in current and real (inflation-adjusted) dollars

The program has two components:

- **CES-National (CES-N):** national estimates by detailed industry (NAICS 2022 basis, currently)
- **CES-State and Area (CES-SA):** estimates for all 50 states, DC, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and roughly 450 metropolitan areas and divisions

Key conceptual points that trip up new users:

- CES counts **jobs, not people** — a person with two jobs is counted twice.
- It **excludes** agriculture, private household workers, the self-employed, and unpaid family workers (the household survey, CPS, covers those).
- The **reference period** is the pay period that includes the 12th of the month.
- Hours and earnings data are published **only for the private sector**; government gets employment only.

---

## 2. Publisher and Governance

**Publishing agency:** U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), an independent principal statistical agency housed within the **U.S. Department of Labor**.

**Cooperative structure:** CES is a **federal–state cooperative program** — one of the oldest in the federal statistical system (the first cooperative agreement, with New York, dates to 1916). BLS funds State Workforce Agencies (SWAs) through Labor Market Information (LMI) cooperative agreements; states historically collected much of the sample data and produce state/area estimates, though BLS has assumed nearly all national data collection (the last state collection transferred to BLS around 2007). BLS gained full financial responsibility for the LMI system in 1983.

**Funding:** Annual congressional appropriations to BLS through the DOL budget, supplemented historically by initiatives like the Federal Economic Indicators (FEI) funding in the 1990s.

**Survey clearance:** The collection instrument (form BLS-790) is cleared by OMB under the Paperwork Reduction Act (OMB control number 1220-0011). Response is **voluntary under federal law**, though some states have mandatory-reporting laws for related employer surveys.

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Organic statute:** The Bureau of Labor Statistics was created in 1884. Its duties are codified at **29 U.S.C. §§ 1–2**. Section 2 contains an explicit monthly mandate: BLS "shall also collect, collate, report, and publish **at least once each month** full and complete statistics of the volume of and changes in employment, as indicated by the number of persons employed, the total wages paid, and the total hours of employment" across specified industries, reported nationally, by state, and by smaller geographic subdivisions as the Secretary prescribes. This is the direct statutory basis for CES.
- **Confidentiality:** Respondent data are protected under the **Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act of 2002 (CIPSEA)**, Title V of the E-Government Act (44 U.S.C. § 3501 note / ch. 35). CIPSEA pledges data will be used for statistical purposes only, imposes criminal penalties for disclosure, and exempts protected data from FOIA. Only aggregate estimates are ever published; **microdata are not publicly available**.
- **Related authorities:** The UI tax records used for the sampling frame and benchmarking flow through state workforce agencies under the Social Security Act (1935) framework; NAICS classification is maintained under OMB's statistical policy directives.

---

## 4. History (condensed from the BLS Handbook of Methods timeline)

CES celebrated its **centennial in 2015** with a series of Monthly Labor Review articles. Key milestones:

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1915** | BLS begins collecting employment/payroll data for 4 manufacturing industries (boots & shoes, cotton goods, cotton finishing, hosiery & underwear), prompted by unfavorable comparison with British, German, and French statistics in the first *Monthly Review* |
| **1916** | First cooperative agreement (New York); expansion to 13 industries, 574 establishments |
| **1923** | Expansion to 52 manufacturing industries, following President Harding's Committee on Employment Statistics |
| **1929–32** | Nonmanufacturing coverage added (34,000 reporters); hours and earnings collection begins; federal civil service reporting begins |
| **1935–36** | Social Security Act creates the UI system — later the benchmark source; **first national total nonfarm wage-and-salary employment estimate (1936)** |
| **1940–45** | WWII-era series for war agencies; War and Navy Departments use earnings indexes in defense-contract escalation clauses |
| **1949** | Cooperative agreements with all 48 states; first comprehensive UI-based benchmark |
| **1950** | Historical reconstruction produces continuous series back to **1919** |
| **1954** | BLS begins publishing **seasonally adjusted** estimates; *Employment and Earnings* periodical begins |
| **1962** | Gordon Commission (JFK) clears the program of political-manipulation charges, recommends methodological improvements |
| **1979** | Levitan Commission criticizes sample design, urges redesign |
| **1982** | Annual benchmarking becomes standard practice |
| **1980s** | CATI and touch-tone data entry introduced; mail "shuttle" form (used since inception) begins phase-out (1983) |
| **1995–2003** | Probability-sample redesign: probability-based stratified sample, **net birth/death model**, NAICS conversion, concurrent seasonal adjustment — fully implemented 2003 |
| **2006–07** | Women-workers series briefly discontinued, then **reinstated after 5,000+ user complaints** — a notable episode for data advocates |
| **2008–11** | Experimental then official **all-employee hours and earnings** series published (a long-requested expansion) |
| **2015** | Centennial; transition to X-13ARIMA-SEATS seasonal adjustment |
| **2020–21** | Temporary COVID-19 adjustments to estimation |
| **2023** | Conversion to **NAICS 2022** |
| **2025** | Birth/death model adjusted mid-year for greater sensitivity to current conditions |

---

## 5. Methodology Snapshot (what a data scientist needs to know)

- **Sampling frame:** The BLS Longitudinal Database (LDB) of employer UI tax records (QCEW universe, ~9+ million UI accounts).
- **Design:** Stratified simple random sample of worksites clustered by UI account; strata by state, industry, and employment size; optimum allocation to minimize variance on total nonfarm employment. Sample redrawn annually with quarterly rotation; business-birth supplemental sample selected mid-year.
- **Collection:** New sample units initiated via computer-assisted telephone interviewing (CATI) for ~5 months, then transitioned to self-initiated modes: web, fax, touch-tone data entry (TDE), or electronic data interchange (EDI).
- **Estimation:** Two-part estimator — (1) a **weighted link-relative estimator** using matched sample reports for month-to-month change, and (2) a **net birth/death model** to account for new firms that can't yet appear in the sample.
- **Seasonal adjustment:** Concurrent seasonal adjustment using X-13ARIMA-SEATS, with special treatments (4- vs. 5-week effect, floating holidays, poll workers in election years, weather outliers in construction).
- **Revision cycle:** First preliminary estimates ~3 weeks after the reference month; revised **twice** in subsequent months; then re-anchored **annually** in the benchmark process to near-universe QCEW counts (final benchmarks released each February with the January Employment Situation). Benchmark revisions are usually small (10-year absolute average ≈ 0.2%), though the preliminary March 2025 benchmark revision of **−911,000 (−0.6%)** — announced September 9, 2025 — was unusually large and politically prominent.
- **Documentation:** The definitive source is the **BLS Handbook of Methods**, CES chapter (https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/), which maintains *archived versions* — itself a preservation-conscious practice. Technical notes: https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cestn.htm.

---

## 6. Data Access, Formats, and Identifiers

All published CES data are **free and in the public domain** (U.S. government work, 17 U.S.C. § 105).

| Access route | Details |
|---|---|
| **Flat files (bulk)** | https://download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/ — tab-delimited text files. `ce.data.0.AllCESSeries` (~350 MB) contains every national series; smaller files are split by supersector. Metadata files: `ce.series`, `ce.industry`, `ce.datatype`, `ce.seasonal`, `ce.footnote`, `ce.txt` (layout documentation). Updated monthly. |
| **BLS Public Data API** | https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v2/ — JSON or Excel output; v1 requires no registration; v2 (registered, free) allows 500 queries/day, 50 series/query, 20 years/call. |
| **Web tools** | Series Report, one-screen/multi-screen data search, "Databases & Tables" at bls.gov/ces/data |
| **News release** | The monthly *Employment Situation* (with CPS data), typically released 8:30 a.m. ET on the first Friday after the reference month, under strict embargo with media lockups |
| **Third-party mirrors** | Federal Reserve **FRED/ALFRED** (e.g., PAYEMS series) — ALFRED notably preserves **vintage (real-time) data**, valuable given CES's revision cycle; also mirrored by BEA, Census, OECD, and countless commercial redistributors |

**Series ID structure** (national): `CE` + seasonal-adjustment code (S/U) + 2-digit supersector + 6-digit industry + 2-digit data type. Example: `CES0000000001` = all employees, total nonfarm, seasonally adjusted, in thousands — the famous "nonfarm payrolls" number, with seasonally adjusted data back to **January 1939** (unadjusted reconstructions to 1919).

**Preservation-friendly traits:** plain-text flat files, stable series IDs, published codebooks, archived documentation, and public-domain status. **Preservation challenges:** the published series are *overwritten* with revisions — historical vintages are not retained by BLS (ALFRED and academic archives fill this gap), and state/metro flat files live in a separate directory (`/pub/time.series/sm/` etc.).

---

## 7. Users and Uses

CES is consistently ranked among the most consequential federal statistics:

- **Monetary policy:** The Federal Reserve weighs payroll employment and average hourly earnings heavily in FOMC decisions.
- **Fiscal and executive policy:** Treasury, Council of Economic Advisers, OMB, CBO, and the President use CES monthly; state and local governments use CES-SA for planning, budgeting, and federal fund allocation formulas.
- **Downstream statistics:** CES is a direct input to BEA's **Personal Income** estimates (aggregate earnings), the Federal Reserve's **Industrial Production** index, The Conference Board's **Index of Leading Economic Indicators** (manufacturing average weekly hours) and **Index of Coincident Indicators** (employment), and BLS **productivity measures**.
- **Financial markets:** The payrolls number is among the most market-moving data releases on earth; bond, equity, and currency markets react within seconds.
- **Business and labor:** Wage escalation clauses (historically in defense contracts), site selection, industry benchmarking; unions use hours/earnings series in negotiations.
- **Research:** Labor economists rely on CES for industry-level wage and employment dynamics; real-time researchers use vintages to study revisions themselves.
- **Media and the public:** The "jobs report" is a fixture of monthly news coverage and political discourse.

---

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **Timeliness:** CES is, together with the unemployment rate, the **first major economic indicator** released each month — an early-warning system for the whole economy.
2. **Breadth and granularity:** 25,000+ published series spanning detailed NAICS industries, all states, and ~450 metro areas, with over a century of continuity.
3. **Quality infrastructure:** Probability sampling, a near-universe benchmark (QCEW), transparent methodology, published error measures, and a documented revision policy.
4. **Accountability:** Independent, professionally produced employment data are a check on political claims about the economy — the 1962 Gordon Commission and 1993 GAO reviews both examined and vindicated the program against manipulation charges.
5. **Free access:** Public-domain data via bulk download and API lowers the barrier for researchers, journalists, small businesses, and civic technologists.

---

## 9. Preservation and Risk Considerations (for preservationists, librarians, and activists)

- **2025 political pressure:** After a weak July 2025 jobs report with large downward revisions, President Trump **fired BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer** (August 1, 2025) alleging — without evidence — manipulated data. The nomination of a partisan successor (later withdrawn), staffing reductions, budget pressures, and the fall 2025 government shutdown (which delayed/suspended releases including the jobs report) all raised alarms among statisticians, economists, and open-data advocates about the continuity and independence of federal economic statistics. The disbanding of federal statistical advisory committees in early 2025 removed another layer of external oversight.
- **Large benchmark revision:** The −911,000 preliminary benchmark for March 2025 intensified political scrutiny, though such revisions are a normal, documented part of the estimation cycle.
- **Response-rate erosion:** First-month collection rates have declined substantially over the past decade-plus, a methodological stress point BLS acknowledges.
- **What to archive:** The monthly flat files at `download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/` (and `sm/`, `sa/` for state/area); the *Employment Situation* news releases and their PDF/HTML archives; the Handbook of Methods CES chapter (including its archived versions); benchmark articles; and technical notes. Because BLS overwrites revised series, **monthly snapshots are essential** to preserve real-time vintages — ALFRED (St. Louis Fed) is the gold-standard complement.
- **Community efforts:** CES content is captured by the Internet Archive, the End of Term Web Archive, and data-rescue initiatives (e.g., the Data Rescue Project, DataLumos at ICPSR) that mobilized around federal-data threats in 2025. Libraries using FRED's API should note it is a redistributor, not an archive of record.
- **Legal durability:** The mandate in 29 U.S.C. § 2 is statutory and explicit ("at least once each month"), meaning discontinuation would require congressional action — but appropriations, staffing, and political independence remain the practical vulnerabilities.

---

## 10. Key Contacts and Further Reading

- Program homepage: https://www.bls.gov/ces (national); https://www.bls.gov/sae (state/metro)
- Technical information: cesinfo@bls.gov, (202) 691-6555
- Handbook of Methods, CES chapter: https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/
- Centennial series, *Monthly Labor Review* (2016): "One hundred years of Current Employment Statistics" (four articles covering data collection, sample design, and survey advancements)
- Technical notes & benchmark documentation: https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cestn.htm; https://www.bls.gov/ces/publications/benchmark/
- Statutory text: 29 U.S.C. §§ 1–2 (via uscode.house.gov or Cornell LII)

**Bottom line:** Your citation is accurate. CES is a 110-year-old, statutorily mandated, federal–state cooperative survey that functions as the nation's first monthly economic indicator. It is exceptionally well documented and freely accessible, but its revision-overwrite publication model, declining response rates, and recent political turbulence make active snapshot archiving and attention to data-rescue infrastructure genuinely worthwhile for anyone in the preservation community.

# Risk Assessment: Current Employment Statistics (CES)

**Assessment date context:** October 2026. Note that a great deal has happened to this program since January 2025, so each category is assessed against both what has already occurred and the forward-looking risk.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone/High Risk:* No evidence. I found no reports of CES historical files being removed from bls.gov. The full time-series archive (`download.bls.gov/pub/time.series/ce/`) remains live, with national series back to 1919 (unadjusted) / 1939 (seasonally adjusted).
- *Moderate Risk:* No evidence of removal of pre-existing data elements. Annual benchmark revisions (e.g., the −911,000 preliminary March 2025 revision announced Sept. 9, 2025) overwrite current estimates but are a documented, normal methodological process applied prospectively, not a deletion of historical data.
- *No Known Issue:* Historical flat files, archived *Employment Situation* releases, archived Handbook of Methods versions, and benchmark documentation all remain accessible. Complementary archives (ALFRED vintages, Internet Archive, Data Rescue Project captures) exist.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**

The November 2025 report (published Dec. 16, 2025) combined October and November payroll data. This meets the letter of "publication skipped."
- *Moderate Risk:* Publication was delayed (Dec. 2025–Feb. 2026 reports ran late, e.g., the Dec. report published Feb. 13, 2026) and one monthly cycle was skipped, but CES payroll data for the gap months was ultimately published — no permanent hole in the establishment-survey series (unlike the household survey's October unemployment rate, which is permanently missing). Since reopening, releases have been on schedule; the July 2026 report was published normally on Aug. 7, 2026.
- *No Known Issue:* The ICR (OMB 1220-0011) is **active, approved March 25, 2025, expiring August 31, 2027** — well clear of any lapse. Releases are currently on time.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** The shutdown-driven cancellation/delay falls in the past cycle, and the series has been made whole and is publishing on time with a valid ICR. However, the skip demonstrably happened, FY2027 appropriations were not finalized as of this writing (a CR/shutdown risk recurs each October), and the administration has shown willingness to use funding lapses for workforce reduction — making recurrence plausible. I stop short of High because the statutory deadline breach was externally caused (appropriations lapse), quickly remediated, and collection authority is secure through August 2027.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk (actual reductions):* BLS-wide degradations are documented: CPI collection was curtailed in three metro areas (April 2025) and nationwide sample reduced (June 2025); ~350 PPI indexes discontinued (August 2025). These are not CES, but they show cuts reaching production. For CES itself, I found **no implemented reduction** in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- *Moderate Risk (emerging risk):* Strong and specific to CES: (a) BLS announced in **April 2026 that budget constraints forced delays to planned 2026 statistical improvements**; (b) first-month survey response/collection rates have been declining for years, inflating revisions (the record May–June 2025 downward revisions, and again large May–June 2026 revisions); (c) staffing attrition concentrated among experienced methodologists risks estimation quality; (d) the FY2027 budget makes staffing reductions permanent and explicitly narrows BLS to "core data series... required by statute," with Employment & Unemployment Statistics activity FTE falling 526 → 461 → 455 (FY25 actual → FY26 enacted → FY27 request) and funding cut $21.6M (−8.6%) in the FY2027 request.
- *No Known Issue:* CES frequency, industry detail (NAICS 2022), and publication schedule are currently intact; the 2025 birth/death model update and benchmark process continue transparently.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** No CES-specific degradation has yet been implemented, but budget documents explicitly prioritize only statutorily required series, planned improvements were canceled in April 2026, and staffing/response-rate pressures are directly degrading estimate reliability (larger revisions). CES's status as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator protects it more than any other BLS program — which is why this is Moderate rather than High.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue:* CES is among the most explicitly mandated data collections in the U.S. Code. **29 U.S.C. § 2** directs BLS to "collect, collate, report, and publish **at least once each month** full and complete statistics of the volume of and changes in employment, as indicated by the number of persons employed, the total wages paid, and the total hours of employment," nationally and by state. The statute is cited verbatim in the ICR's supporting statement (the Title 29 USC 1-2 PDF is attached to the 2025 ICR package). CES is a designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator, feeds statutory formulas (BEA Personal Income, Fed Industrial Production, leading/coincident indexes), and has **no substitute**: the household survey (CPS) measures people, not jobs; QCEW is quarterly and lagged ~6 months; ADP is private and methodologically distinct. Terminating or gutting CES would require amending a statute on the books since 1884.

**Rating: No Known Issue.** This is the strongest anchor of protection the dataset has — and notably, the administration's own FY2027 budget justification invokes statutory requirement as the criterion for what to preserve, which puts CES first in line for protection.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk (≥40% staff, ≥1,000 staff, ≥20% budget, or leadership removed):* **Leadership was removed** — Commissioner Erika McEntarfer was fired August 1, 2025 over unfavorable jobs numbers, and the agency ran under an acting commissioner for over a year. Senior-leadership hollowing: **more than a third of senior-level positions were vacant at the start of 2026**, per reporting at Matsumoto's confirmation. DOL overall lost ~2,700 employees (~20%).
- *Moderate Risk (10–39% staff, 10–19% budget, threatened leadership change):* BLS direct FTE fell from **2,019 (FY2025 actual) to 1,773 (FY2026 enacted) ≈ −12%**, with the FY2027 request at 1,754 and the budget explicitly "making permanent recent staffing reductions." Reports during the 2025 DOGE layoffs/deferred resignations described BLS losing roughly 10–25% of staff. Budget: FY2026 enacted ($708.5M) was roughly flat vs. FY2025 ($704.0M), but the **FY2027 request is $668.0M, −5.7%**, with the Employment & Unemployment Statistics activity cut ~8.6%. Mitigating: the Senate confirmed **Brett Matsumoto, a career BLS research economist, as Commissioner on Aug. 7, 2026** (51–47); he is broadly respected by former commissioners of both parties, pledged science-driven decisions, and the agency is backfilling some vacancies.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable — staff losses clearly exceed 10% and leadership was removed.

**Rating: High Risk.** The rubric makes "leadership removed" alone sufficient for High, and that occurred (Aug. 2025 firing + 12-month vacancy under an acting head), compounded by ~12% FTE loss, one-third of senior positions vacant, and a budget trajectory that locks in the reductions. The August 2026 confirmation of a well-qualified career insider is genuine mitigation — if this assessment were rerun in mid-2027 with no further departures, this category could plausibly downgrade to Moderate.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk:* Elements exist nearby: the commissioner firing was a Presidential Action targeting this exact data product; Trump's first replacement nominee, E.J. Antoni, was a Heritage/Project 2025-aligned BLS critic who had **publicly proposed suspending the monthly jobs report**; Project 2025 calls for consolidating BLS into a single statistical agency; the administration disbanded BLS's advisory committees (Feb. 2025); and the White House's shutdown-era RIF memo (Sept. 24, 2025) targeted programs "not consistent with the President's priorities." However, none of these translated into an actual change to the CES ICR or to what CES collects/publishes: the March 2025 ICR action was a routine nonsubstantive change (Ohio mandatory-reporting note), not a Presidential-Action-driven collection, and no negative policy note appears on the CES pages.
- *Moderate Risk:* Squarely met: **proposed/pending changes** — the President's FY2026 *and* FY2027 budgets carry a live proposal to reorganize BLS, Census, and BEA into a consolidated statistical agency at the Department of Commerce under the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs; and **statements by administration officials** — the President has repeatedly called the jobs numbers "rigged"/"VERY inaccurate" and posted that the BLS had been "FAILING American Businesses," while nominating (then withdrawing) a commissioner candidate who wanted to suspend the monthly report.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable given the above, even though the CES data product itself is unchanged since January 2025.

**Rating: Moderate Risk.** What CES collects and publishes has not been altered — the July 2026 jobs report, released hours before Matsumoto's confirmation, contained large downward revisions and was published normally, which is encouraging evidence of intact professional practice. But the explicit, repeated, budget-documented reorganization proposal and sustained presidential hostility toward this specific data product go well beyond "no notable changes."

---

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | No Known Issue | Full archive (1919–present) intact and accessible; no removals detected |
| **Future Data Availability** | Moderate Risk | Oct. 2025 report canceled and releases delayed during shutdown, since remediated; ICR active through 8/31/2027; recurring appropriations risk |
| **Data Quality** | Moderate Risk | No CES-specific cuts yet, but planned improvements canceled (Apr. 2026), declining response rates enlarging revisions, budget narrowing to statutory minimums |
| **Statutory Context** | No Known Issue | Explicit monthly mandate in 29 U.S.C. § 2; PFEI; no substitute exists |
| **Staffing and Funding** | High Risk | Commissioner fired Aug. 2025; ~12% FTE loss (2,019→1,773); >1/3 of senior positions vacant; cuts made permanent in FY2027 request — partially mitigated by Aug. 2026 confirmation of career insider Matsumoto |
| **Policy** | Moderate Risk | Data collection/publication unchanged, but live reorganization-to-Commerce proposal, repeated presidential attacks on the numbers, and a withdrawn nominee who proposed suspending the monthly report |

**Overall judgment:** CES is the best-protected dataset at BLS — statutorily mandated, a Principal Federal Economic Indicator, irreplaceable, and currently publishing on schedule with a valid ICR and a newly confirmed, well-regarded commissioner. Its risk profile is driven less by what has happened to the data itself (which remains intact and unaltered) than by the demonstrated willingness of the executive branch to fire leadership over its content, the locking-in of ~12% staffing losses, and an unresolved consolidation proposal. The single most important preservation action remains what it was before 2025: **monthly snapshot archiving of the flat files and releases**, since BLS's revision-overwrite model means the published archive does not preserve real-time vintages.
